title: Infrastructure and risk
summary: How to build the business underneath your campaigns: verified identity, healthy accounts, reliable payments, honest appeals and backups that stay inside platform rules. You will also learn why buying or renting accounts, farming, cloaking and ban evasion end operations, and how compliance, a real company, clear contracts and clean records protect everything you scale.

lessons.title: Build on a verified business identity
objectives: By the end you can explain why a verified business is the foundation of every account you run.
By the end you can set up business ownership, admin roles and security the right way.
By the end you can estimate what a single point of failure would cost your operation.

steps.p: At small budgets, one person and one ad account can work. At scale, the accounts, pages, payment methods and people with access become the business itself. If they are fragile, everything you built on top of them is fragile too.

d.s: Build them like an asset, not a tool

steps.say: When you're small, one person and one ad account can work. But at scale, the accounts, pages, payment methods and the people with access become the business itself. As the screen says, your accounts are your factory. If they're fragile, everything you built on top of them is fragile too. So build them like an asset, not a tool.

steps.h: The layers of a clean setup
steps.p: Every serious operation has the same layers. Each one must belong to you or your company, be verified where the platform asks, and be documented so the business does not depend on one person's phone.
d: Legal entity|the company that owns everything
Business portfolio|the platform's container for assets
People and roles|who can do what
Payment methods|in the business's own name
steps.say: Look at these layers. Every serious operation has them. The legal entity, the company that owns everything. The business portfolio, the platform's container for your assets. Ad accounts, where spend happens. Pages and domains, what users see. People and roles, who can do what. And payment methods, in the business's own name. Each layer must belong to you or your company, be verified where asked, and be documented, so the business doesn't depend on one person's phone.

steps.p: Order matters. Verification is far easier when the legal entity, website and contact details already match. Tool names change: at the time of writing Meta calls what was Business Manager a business portfolio. Check the current help pages before you start.
steps.say: Order matters here. Follow the flow: register the company, create the business portfolio, verify the business, verify your domain, add ad accounts and pages, and then assign roles. Why this order? Verification is far easier when the legal entity, website and contact details already match. At the time of writing, Meta calls what was Business Manager a business portfolio, but tool names change, so check the current help pages before you start.

steps.p: Platforms ask you to prove the business is real and that you represent it. Exact documents vary by country and change over time, so check the current requirements before you start. Matching details across documents is what most often decides success.
d: Legal business name exactly as registered
Registration document from the company registry
Business address and phone that match
A live website on your own domain
A business email on that domain
An authorised person with valid ID
steps.say: Platforms ask you to prove the business is real and that you represent it. Here's what's usually needed. The legal business name exactly as registered. A registration document from the company registry. A business address and phone that match. A live website on your own domain. A business email on that domain. And an authorised person with valid I D. Documents vary by country and change over time, so check current requirements. Matching details is what most often decides success.

steps.p: A common reason verification fails is small mismatches: a different spelling of the company name, an old address, or a website that does not show the business name. Fix the mismatch before resubmitting rather than trying again and hoping.

d.text: Put your registered company name and contact details in the website footer before you apply.

steps.say: A common reason verification fails is a small mismatch. A different spelling of the company name, an old address, or a website that doesn't show the business name. When that happens, fix the mismatch before you resubmit. Don't just try again and hope. And here's a simple tip: put your registered company name and contact details in your website footer before you apply.

steps.p: Give each person the least access they need to do their job. Admin rights are powerful: an admin can remove other admins. Role names change; check the current platform.
steps.more: Keep at least two trusted admins who are real people in the company, each with two-factor authentication. If the only admin loses their phone, leaves, or has their personal profile restricted, the whole business can be locked out. When someone leaves, remove their access the same day and record it.
steps.say: Give each person the least access they need. Look at the table. Business admin is for the founder plus one deputy, and can do everything, including managing people. Media buyers get advertiser access to create and edit ads. Reporting staff get analyst access, view only. And your accountant gets finance access for billing. Admin rights are powerful, because an admin can remove other admins. Keep at least two trusted admins, each with two-factor authentication, and remove leavers the same day. Role names change, so check the current platform.

steps.p: Most account losses at scale are not policy bans. They are hacked profiles and lost access. These basics prevent most of them and cost almost nothing.
d: A password manager for the team
Never share logins; add people properly
steps.say: Here's something many people don't expect. Most account losses at scale aren't policy bans. They're hacked profiles and lost access. These basics prevent most of them and cost almost nothing. Two-factor authentication for every person. An authenticator app, not only S M S. A password manager for the team. Business email, not personal Gmail. Remove leavers the same day. And never share logins, add people properly.

steps.p: Write access rules with clear numbers so nobody has to judge them on a busy day. These are starting rules; adapt them to the size of your team, and check the platform's current role options because names and limits change.

rows: At least 2 real people, few more
All access removed the same day

steps.say: Write access rules with clear numbers, so nobody has to judge them on a busy day. Look at the starting lines. Business admins: at least two real people, and few more. Two-factor: every person, checked monthly. Leavers: all access removed the same day. New people: least role first, raise later. And a people audit monthly and after any incident. Adapt these to your team size, and check the platform's current role options, because names and limits change.

steps.h: Worked example: one point of failure
steps.p: Example: your operation makes $600 a day in profit through one business portfolio with one admin. That admin's profile is hacked and the business is locked for 10 days while you recover it. The direct cost is $6,000 in lost profit.

d.label: profit lost in 10 days of lockout

steps.more: The real cost is higher. Campaigns that relaunch often need time to stabilise again, the network may give your cap to other affiliates while you are out, and your team is paid while they wait. Compare that with the cost of a second admin, two-factor authentication and a password manager: close to zero.

steps.h: Common mistakes: built to burn vs to last
steps.p: Two ways to set up the same operation. The left column lists the mistakes we see most; it feels faster in week one. The right column is the fix for each, and the only setup still running in year two.

b.title: Built to last
items: Each person has their own access

steps.say: Here are two ways to set up the same operation. On the left, built to burn: accounts in other people's names, one shared login, personal cards, and no verification. It feels faster in week one. On the right, built to last: everything owned by your company, each person with their own access, business payment methods, and business and domain verified. That's the only setup still running in year two.

steps.p: Running ads through accounts in another person's name, whether bought, rented or borrowed, breaks platform terms and can break laws on fraud and identity misuse. It also means someone else can take your business away at any time.

d.text: Every account you advertise from should belong to you or your company, in your real details.

steps.say: This is a firm line. Running ads through accounts in another person's name, whether bought, rented or borrowed, breaks platform terms, and can break laws on fraud and identity misuse. It also means someone else can take your business away at any time. As the warning says, every account you advertise from should belong to you or your company, in your real details.

steps.p: Verified businesses with long, clean histories tend to get more trust from platforms over time. That trust is hard to fake and slow to build, which is exactly why it protects you from competitors who cut corners.

d.s: Every month of good behaviour adds to it

steps.say: Here's why this is worth it. Verified businesses with long, clean histories tend to get more trust from platforms over time. That trust is hard to fake and slow to build. And that's exactly why it protects you from competitors who cut corners. As the screen says, clean history compounds. Every month of good behaviour adds to it.

lessons.title: Account health and account quality
objectives: By the end you can read the signals that show an ad account's health.
By the end you can track your disapproval rate and act before it becomes a restriction.
By the end you can build habits that keep accounts in good standing at scale.

steps.p: Platforms judge an account by its history: the ads it submitted, how many were rejected, how users responded, whether payments succeeded and whether it followed the rules. Every day either adds to that record or takes from it.

d.b: Every ad is a vote on your account
d.s: Good history builds trust; violations spend it

steps.say: Platforms judge an account by its history. The ads it submitted, how many were rejected, how users responded, whether payments succeeded, and whether it followed the rules. As the screen says, every ad is a vote on your account. Good history builds trust, and violations spend it. So every single day either adds to that record or takes from it.

steps.p: Platforms do not publish exact formulas, and they change. These are the broad areas that matter, according to their own help pages and common experience. Treat each one as something you can manage.
d: Landing pages|what happens after the click
steps.say: Look at these cards. Platforms don't publish exact formulas, and they change. But these are the broad areas that matter. Your policy record, meaning rejections and violations. User feedback, like hides, reports and negative comments. Payments, failed charges and disputes. Landing pages, what happens after the click. And security, unusual logins and access. Treat each one as something you can manage.

steps.p: Most platforms have a page that shows the status of your assets. At the time of writing Meta calls it Account Quality; it lists restrictions and lets you request a review. Names and locations change, and we are not certain they are current; check the current Ads Manager.
steps.say: So where do you look? At the time of writing, Meta calls its status page Account Quality. It lists restrictions and lets you request a review. Look at the table. Check rejected ads in Ads Manager daily. Restrictions on the account status page, daily. User feedback in ad and page comments, daily. Payment issues in billing, weekly. And landing page errors with your own monitoring, daily. Names and locations change, so check the current Ads Manager.

steps.p: This one number gives you an early warning. A rising disapproval rate usually comes before restrictions, not after. Track it weekly for each account and each buyer.
steps.say: Here's one number that gives you an early warning: your disapproval rate. It's ads rejected, divided by ads submitted. Why does it matter? A rising disapproval rate usually comes before restrictions, not after. So track it weekly, for each account and for each buyer.

steps.p: Example: your team submitted 40 ads this week and 6 were rejected. That is 6 ÷ 40 = 15%. Last month it was 5%. Something changed in how ads are being written or what the landing pages say.
steps.more: There is no published safe number, and it varies by vertical. What matters is your trend and the reasons. Group rejections by the policy named in the notice. If most are for the same reason, such as claims about results, you have one problem to fix in your creative brief, not six separate accidents.
steps.say: Here's a worked example. Your team submitted forty ads this week, and six were rejected. Six divided by forty is fifteen percent, the number on screen. Last month it was five percent. That tells you something changed, in how ads are written or what the landing pages say. There's no published safe number, and it varies by vertical. What matters is your trend and the reasons behind it.

steps.p: Example: grouping a month of rejections shows where the problem really is. Here, one reason accounts for more than half, so one change to the brief fixes most of it.

And other reasons, two. One reason accounts for more than half. So one change to the creative brief fixes most of the problem. That's why you group by reason, not just count.

steps.p: One tab, one row per ad account, filled every Monday from the rejection notices. The rate column is a formula. The reason field is what you act on: one repeated reason means one fix to the brief. Example figures.

steps.p: No platform publishes a safe disapproval rate, so these lines use your own history. Example: if your usual rate is 5%, a week at 10% or more triggers the stricter review. Starting rules; adapt them to your vertical and data.

rows: Treat as a hack: secure first

Rate up two weeks running: fix the brief before new launches. Rate at two times your baseline or more: second-person review on every ad. Same reason three or more times: update the claims register. Unknown login: treat it as a hack and secure first. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your vertical and data.

steps.p: Reviews look at what happens after the click. A clean ad that sends users to a page with income promises, fake countdowns or broken links will still hurt the account.

d.text: The ad and the page must say the same honest thing. Never show reviewers one page and users another.

steps.say: Reviews look at what happens after the click, not just at the ad. A clean ad that sends users to a page with income promises, fake countdowns or broken links will still hurt the account. As the warning says, the ad and the page must say the same honest thing. Never show reviewers one page and users another.

steps.p: Five minutes a day is enough to catch most problems early, while they are cheap to fix. Assign this to one named person so it does not fall between buyers.
d: Test landing pages on a phone
steps.say: Five minutes a day catches most problems early, while they're cheap to fix. Here's the daily routine. Check the status page for restrictions. Read every rejection notice. Hide spam and answer real questions. Test landing pages on a phone. And log unusual logins or changes. Assign this to one named person, so it doesn't fall between buyers.

steps.p: Example: the named health owner posts one short message in the team chat each morning. It says what was checked, what was found and what was done, so buyers do not have to open every status page themselves.

Paused that angle. Brief updated: no daily earnings lines. Lander checked on a phone, loads fine.
Thanks. I will rewrite both from the claims register and send them for review.

steps.say: In this chat, the named health owner posts one short message each morning. Notice what it covers. No restrictions. Two ads rejected on one account, both for outcome claims. That angle is paused, the brief is updated with no daily earnings lines, and the lander is checked on a phone. A teammate replies that they'll rewrite both from the claims register. Now nobody else has to open every status page.

lessons.title: Payments, billing and spending limits
objectives: By the end you can explain billing thresholds, spending limits and why payments fail at scale.
By the end you can plan payment capacity before you raise budgets.
By the end you can account for currency costs in your true CPA.

steps.h: Payments are part of account health
steps.p: A failed payment is not just an admin problem. Repeated failed charges can pause delivery, lower trust in the account and in some cases lead to restrictions. At scale, payment capacity is as important as creative.

d.b: A declined card can stop a winner
d.s: Plan payment capacity like you plan budget

steps.say: A failed payment isn't just an admin problem. Repeated failed charges can pause delivery, lower trust in the account, and in some cases lead to restrictions. As the screen says, a declined card can stop a winner. So at scale, plan your payment capacity just like you plan your budget. It's as important as creative.

steps.p: Three different limits often get confused. Each one works differently and is set by a different party. Names and rules vary by platform and country; check the current billing help.
d: Billing threshold|spend level that triggers a charge
Account spending limit|a cap you set on total spend
Card or bank limit|what your bank allows per day
steps.say: Three different limits often get confused. Look at the cards. The billing threshold is the spend level that triggers a charge. The account spending limit is a cap you set on total spend. And the card or bank limit is what your bank allows per day. Each works differently and is set by a different party. Names and rules vary by platform and country, so check the current billing help.

steps.p: On many platforms, at the time of writing, you are charged each time spend reaches a billing threshold, and also on a regular billing date. Thresholds often start low and may rise with good payment history. We are not certain how your account is set; check its billing page.

d.text: More spend with the same threshold means more charges per day, and more chances for a bank to flag one.

steps.say: Here's how thresholds work on many platforms, at the time of writing. You're charged each time spend reaches the billing threshold, and also on a regular billing date. Thresholds often start low and may rise with good payment history. We're not certain how your account is set, so check its billing page. And here's the key point on screen: more spend with the same threshold means more charges per day, and more chances for a bank to flag one.

steps.p: Example: your billing threshold is $250 and you spend $1,000 a day. You will be charged about four times a day. If your bank flags repeated foreign charges as suspicious, one of them may be declined.
steps.say: Let's do the maths. In this example, your billing threshold is two hundred and fifty dollars, and you spend one thousand dollars a day. One thousand divided by two hundred and fifty is about four charges a day, the number on screen. If your bank flags repeated foreign charges as suspicious, one of those four may be declined.

steps.h: Worked example: will the card hold?
steps.p: Example: a business card with a $1,500 daily limit. At each budget level, compare daily spend with the card limit. The plan breaks before the campaign does.
steps.more: Many operators keep spend below about 70% of the daily card limit as a rough guide, to leave room for timing, taxes and other charges on the same card. Here that means about $1,050 a day. To go higher, talk to your bank about a higher limit or add a second payment method owned by the same business.
steps.say: Will the card hold? In this example, a business card has a fifteen hundred dollar daily limit. At six hundred a day, you have nine hundred room left. At one thousand, five hundred left. At fourteen hundred, only one hundred. And at eighteen hundred, you're three hundred over, so it fails. The plan breaks before the campaign does. As a rough guide, many operators keep spend below about seventy percent of the card limit, here about one thousand and fifty dollars a day.

steps.p: Use payment methods in your company's name, with a backup ready before you need it. Options vary by country and platform, so check what is available for your business.

A backup method on the same business
Bank told to expect regular foreign charges
Limits checked before each budget step

steps.p: Automated review makes mistakes, and so do people. A restriction is not always a sign you did something wrong. The way you respond, calmly and with evidence, decides how quickly you recover and whether your record stays clean.

d.s: A good appeal is short, specific and honest

steps.say: Automated review makes mistakes, and so do people. So a restriction isn't always a sign you did something wrong. What matters is how you respond. Calmly, and with evidence. As the screen says, respond with evidence, not anger. A good appeal is short, specific and honest, and it decides how quickly you recover and whether your record stays clean.

steps.p: Most platforms offer a way to request a review from the status page of the restricted asset. Steps and names change; check the current help pages. Read the notice carefully before doing anything. Full step-by-step, with templates: Ad account bans module.
steps.say: Here's the appeal process. Follow the flow. Read the exact notice. Check the named policy. Fix what's genuinely wrong. Request a review. Then record the outcome. Most platforms let you request a review from the status page of the restricted asset, but steps and names change, so check the current help pages. The full step-by-step, with templates, is in the Ad account bans module.

steps.p: Example: a short, factual message to support after an ad was rejected. It names the asset, explains the change, and asks one clear question. It does not argue or threaten.

d.text: Hello. Ad ID 1234 was rejected under the policy on unrealistic outcomes.
We removed the line 'earn daily' and now say 'learn how trading works; trading involves risk'. The landing page says the same.
Our business is verified and the offer is authorised for this country. Could you review the updated ad?

steps.say: Look at this example appeal message. It names the rejected ad and the policy, unrealistic outcomes. Then it explains the change: the line earn daily was removed, and replaced with learn how trading works, trading involves risk, and the landing page says the same. It notes the business is verified and the offer is authorised for the country. Then it asks one clear question. Notice it doesn't argue or threaten.

steps.p: Reviewers handle many cases a day. Make yours easy to approve by giving them everything they need in one place, in plain words, without long stories or emotion.

Why it now meets the policy

Proof of authorization if the offer is regulated. And one clear request. Put it all in one place, in plain words, without long stories or emotion.

steps.h: Do not fix and appeal at the same time on a guess
steps.p: If you do not understand why something was rejected, read the policy first. Appealing an ad that genuinely breaks the rules wastes the review and adds to your record.

d.text: If it breaks the policy, edit it. If you believe it does not, appeal it with your reason.

steps.p: Every restriction ends in one of three decisions. Use these lines so the decision does not depend on your mood. Starting rules; the platform's current options decide what is available, so check the notice and the help pages.
steps.say: Every restriction ends in one of three decisions: fix, appeal or accept. Look at the table. If the ad breaks the named policy, fix it and don't appeal. If you believe it complies, appeal once, with evidence. If an ad appeal is denied, rewrite or drop the angle. If a business appeal is denied, accept it, and open no new accounts. And if one platform is over eighty percent of profit, start a second-source test. These are starting rules, and the platform's current options decide what's available.

steps.p: Appeals fail for the same few reasons. Each mistake below makes a reviewer's job harder or adds to your record. Fix them in your template once and every future appeal is better.

Appealing on a guess|read the policy first

steps.p: Redundancy is smart. These backups are generally within platform rules when they are owned by your verified business and used for real business needs, not to evade enforcement. Check current limits.

Owned audiences|email lists and channels you built with consent

These are generally within platform rules when owned by your verified business and used for real needs, not to evade enforcement. Check current limits.

steps.h: The shortcuts we refuse, and why
steps.p: Some sellers market these as 'infrastructure'. They are not. Each one breaks platform terms and often the law, and each ends with the operation losing everything built on it.

rows: Links back to you; wider bans

steps.more: Platforms link accounts using many signals, so evasion often leads to bans spreading to every connected asset, including your legitimate ones. Using another person's identity can break fraud and identity laws in many countries. Cloaking deceives both the platform and users and can be treated as consumer fraud. Networks also terminate affiliates caught doing this and may hold or claw back payouts.
steps.say: Some sellers market these shortcuts as infrastructure. They aren't. Buying or renting accounts means using accounts in other people's names, leading to bans and identity misuse. Account farming mass-creates fake profiles. Cloaking shows reviewers a different page, which is deception with legal risk. And ban evasion creates new assets after a restriction, which links back to you and widens bans. Each breaks platform terms and often the law, and networks may terminate affiliates and hold payouts.

steps.h: Compliance is a process, not a person

steps.say: With one buyer and ten ads a week, the founder can check everything. But with five buyers and a hundred ads a week, compliance has to be a process. steps.p: Every ad and landing page passes through the same steps. The reviewer is not the person who made the ad. Keep the record so you can show what was checked.
steps.say: Here's a review pipeline. Follow the flow. A brief with approved claims. The creative is made. A second person reviews it. Fix or approve. Launch. And log the decision. steps.p: A claims register is a short list of what you may and may not say about each offer, agreed with the network and checked against platform policy and local law. Buyers write from it instead of guessing.
